Subject: Residency routing options & backups — follow-up from today's discussion

Hi Ellen / HealthCore team,

Thanks for taking the time today — appreciate the clear priorities. Quick recap from our side and proposed next steps so we can align on residency, failover, and logging requirements: 

Call recap (high level):
- Primary ask: ensure customer data for HealthCore accounts is pinned to a US region with predictable failover behavior for DR.
- Compliance note: HealthCore will treat model inputs containing patient PII as sensitive; Legal asked about auditability and retention windows.
- Operational ask: minimal cross-region replication unless required for DR; prefer warm-standby approach to reduce cross-region exposure.

Options we suggest (trade-offs):
1) Per-tenant single-region pin (recommended baseline)
   - Behavior: All inference traffic and persisted artifacts (logs, backups) remain in chosen region (US-East).
   - Pros: simplest compliance posture, lowest cross-region data movement.
   - Cons: longer recovery if region outage; RTO depends on restore time from backups.

2) Primary region + warm standby in another region
   - Behavior: Primary operates in US-East; snapshots of persisted state and backups are replicated to US-West warm-standby.
   - Pros: faster recovery, limited cross-region replication of backups only, controlled failover.
   - Cons: additional cost for standby capacity and cross-region storage; KV cache cannot be live-synced (see below).

3) Multi-region active (not recommended for PII-heavy workloads)
   - Behavior: Active-active replication of requests/data across regions.
   - Pros: lowest latency globally; highest cost and complexity.
   - Cons: increases surface area for data residency/compliance.

PII & logging controls (quick notes):
- Encryption: data at rest and in transit is encrypted (default AWS KMS). We can support customer-managed KMS keys per-region under Private/Dedicated deployments.
- Logging: Access logs and operational traces can be configured to redact user-level PII; raw debug logs that include request payloads are stored only if explicitly enabled and can be retained for a configurable window.
- Backups: snapshot-based backups can be retained per-customer for X days (default 30). We can extend retention on request.

Immediate asks for HealthCore to move forward:
- Confirm target RTO and RPO targets for the HealthCore tenant (examples: RTO 2 hours / RPO 24 hours).
- Confirm whether backups are allowed to be stored in a different US region (if warm-standby is acceptable).
- Confirm whether customer-managed KMS is required.

Attachments: I attached a one-page diagram (residency-routing-v1.png) and a runbook stub link. I'll also upload a short quote for warm-standby options.

Next steps I propose:
- HealthCore to confirm RTO/RPO + KMS requirement by EOD Friday.
- We prepare a short runbook + updated quote (will include cost delta for warm-standby and retention changes).
- 30-min technical follow-up next week to walk through the runbook and SOC2 artifacts.

Thanks again — happy to get this into a formal doc if helpful.

Best,

Jordan — good writeup. A few quick internal notes to add before we send the runbook/quote: 

- Private vs Dedicated: if HealthCore needs customer-managed KMS keys per region we should push Private (VPC) or Customer-Managed-Dedicated. That path requires a short compliance checklist but gives them control over keys.
- Timeline: config-level region pinning + canary rollout (no infra change) ~ 1-2 weeks; if we need dedicated warm-standby infra it's 3-5 weeks to provision and validate (depends on capacity commitment).
- Pricing: warm-standby typically ~30-40% of primary capacity cost (hot standby is more). I'll draft estimates for the quote.

Quick technical notes for the runbook/quote: 

- KV cache: we do not support live multi-region KV cache replication for model inference. For warm-standby we recommend periodic encrypted snapshots of the KV cache (snapshot frequency configurable) and an automated restore on failover. RTT/throughput during failover will need warming (cold cache warmup).
- Backups: we can configure incremental snapshots to replicate to a secondary US region. Retention configurable per-customer; default retention is 30 days.
- Logging: request-level payloads can be excluded from operational logs; we can store just metadata+hashes for auditability. If HealthCore needs full payloads in logs we need explicit sign-off and it should count as "logged PII".
- Failover mechanics: automated failover is possible but we recommend a manual/controlled failover for the first two incidents to validate behavior; afterward the customer can opt into automatic policy-based failover.

I'll add these as concrete items in the runbook and include a short checklist for the QA/ops validation steps.

-Ben
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Ellen — answering inline and attaching the runbook + quote: 

1) Audit logs: by default request-level logs capture metadata (timestamp, caller id, model, route) and a request hash. Full request payloads are NOT stored in operational logs unless debug logging is explicitly enabled by the customer. We'll provide a short redaction statement for Legal to sign off on.

2) Backups/snapshots: we replicate encrypted snapshots only. For cross-region replication to be allowed we require customer-managed KMS if HealthCore wants to control keys. We'll note that in the quote.

3) Runbook: attached is a 2-page runbook (redwood-region-failover-runbook.pdf) that includes estimated timings: snapshot restore ~ 45-90 minutes depending on snapshot size; cache warmup variable — we recommend a staged traffic re-route and shadow warmup window of ~1-2 hours. We recommend manual confirmation for the first failover.
